an0963.user: Skincare brand, running Google Search mostly. My ads have been spending ₹15L over the last 30 days and honestly I think Google's reporting is just lying to me. How do I figure out which number is the real one so I know if these ads actually work?
an0963.assistant:
Neither dashboard is broken, and that's the part you have to accept first. They're both right and both wrong — they're just answering different questions.

The platform's 4.5 is modelled conversions on a generous click window, so it claims credit for anything it touched, including buyers who'd have come anyway. Shopify last-click at 1.3 only credits the final tap, so it strips out every assist and undercounts. Post-iOS, this gap is structural — it will never close. You're refereeing a fight between two biased witnesses, and the truth sits somewhere in the middle.

Stop trying to pick a winner. Anchor on a number neither platform can spin: blended CAC. Take your full ₹15L spend and divide by the actual count of new customers Shopify recorded this month — not new orders, new customers. That single figure tells you what it really costs to buy a buyer, regardless of which dashboard is grandstanding. Manage to that, set a target you can survive at your margin, and let the two ROAS numbers argue in the corner.

Caveat: blended CAC blurs channels together, so if you're running anything besides Search you'll need to hold spend roughly steady to read the trend cleanly. But it's the honest number, and it's the one you can actually steer by.

Here's the math on why: at ~100 conversions, the confidence band around any rate is wide enough that a 12% swing in either direction is well inside normal week-to-week variance. You'd see this same jitter even if literally nothing changed in your ads, your audience, or the auction. Reacting to it means you'll reset learning, kill a fine campaign, and then panic again next week when it bounces back the other way.

What would actually count as a real shift: the same direction holding for 3-4 consecutive weeks, or a single jump big enough to obviously clear the noise — think CAC up 40-50%, not 12%. Until you see one of those, your job this week is to do nothing and let the data accumulate.

The one caveat: if you know of a real cause — you just slashed budget, a key creative got rejected, festive demand dropped off — then it's not noise and you read it differently. Absent a known trigger, this is variance. Sit on your hands.
